mainTopic: What heirs owe for property their father took: stolen goods, רבית money, and a borrowed cow.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an answer that defends רמי בר חמא's rule that an heir is like a buyer: heirs must return a stolen item only before the owner gave up hope (לפני יאוש). Then רב אדא בר אהבה gives another version, in which רמי בר חמא learned his rule from a ברייתא saying heirs need not return רבית money. רבא rejects that proof, because the Torah commands only the lender himself to return רבית, not his son. Next, two ברייתות discuss a thief's children who eat or inherit stolen food. רבא and רב פפא each reread one of them so it makes sense. רבא then rules on heirs left a borrowed cow, and the גמרא connects his ruling to רב פפא's view about when a borrower becomes liable. A third ברייתא learns from 'אשר גזל' that the actual stolen item must be returned, and it brings סומכוס's view that minors are exempt. The amud ends with a story: רבי ירמיה's brother-in-law shuts him out of a house, and רבי אבין's response continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the answer for רמי בר חמא: the case is before despair
steps.stepSummary: The last words of the answer from the previous discussion, which defends רמי בר חמא's view: the ברייתא where the heirs must return the item is talking about before יאוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The case where they must return it is] before the owners gave up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: These two words finish the answer from just before this section, which defends רמי בר חמא's view. The case where heirs must give back the stolen item is one where the owner had not yet given up hope (לפני יאוש).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if an heir is like a buyer, a change of ownership only acquires the item after the owner has given up hope. Before יאוש, the item still belongs to the owner, so the heirs never acquired it and must return it. That is why the ברייתא obligating heirs does not contradict רמי בר חמא.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner giving up hope of getting his lost or stolen property back

phrases.english: Before despair.
phrases.notes: 'Despair' means the owner has given up hope of getting it back. This finishes the answer above about when the heirs must pay back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer defending רמי בר חמא's view, which began before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case narrowing: placing the case at a specific time (before יאוש)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא that obligates heirs to pay seems to contradict the rule that an heir's ownership is like a buyer's.
steps.terutzMaskana: Heirs are like buyers, but they acquire only after יאוש; the ברייתא that obligates them is before יאוש.

steps.title: Second version: רמי בר חמא's rule taught on the רבית ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה places רמי בר חמא's statement on a ברייתא instead. Heirs who inherit רבית money do not have to return it, even when they know it is רבית. From this, רמי בר חמא learns that an heir's ownership is like a buyer's.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה teaches רמי בר חמא's statement on this ברייתא: If their father left them money from interest, even if they know it is interest money, they don't have to return it. רמי בר חמא said: this shows that an heir's ownership is like a buyer's ownership.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different tradition about where רמי בר חמא's rule came from. In this version he learned it from a ברייתא about inherited רבית money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא exempts the heirs even though they know the money came from רבית. רמי בר חמא explains why: the money passed into the heirs' possession, just as if they had bought it. That change of ownership frees them from returning it.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches (here: attaches a statement to a specific source)
Interest on a loan, which the Torah forbids
The ownership or domain of an heir
The ownership or domain of a buyer

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion of רמי בר חמא. It is the same rule, but this version says it was learned from a different source: a ברייתא about רבית instead of the משנה.
steps.whyThisMatters: Whether an heir counts like a buyer decides whether heirs must return things their father took wrongfully.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches
this statement of Rami bar Ḥama on this [source]:

phrases.aramaic: הִנִּיחַ לָהֶן אֲבִיהֶן מָעוֹת שֶׁל רִבִּית,
phrases.english: If their father left them money of interest,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדְעִין שֶׁהֵן שֶׁל רִבִּית –
phrases.english: even though they know that it is from interest –
they are not obligated to return it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא, זֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת:
phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said: That is to say:
the domain of an heir is like the domain of a buyer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה מַתְנֵי לְהָא דְּרָמֵי בַּר חָמָא אַהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of where רמי בר חמא's rule was taught.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Heirs need not return inherited רבית money, and רמי בר חמא learns from this that an heir's ownership is like a buyer's.

steps.title: רבא: the interest case is special because of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the proof. Heirs do not have to return רבית because the duty to return it comes from a פסוק that commands only the lender himself. It has nothing to do with heirs being like buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Really, I can tell you that an heir's ownership is not like a buyer's. Here it is different, because the פסוק says: 'Do not take from him interest or increase.' Return it to him so that he can live with you. The Torah warns the lender himself. It does not warn his son.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רמי בר חמא's proof. He gives a different reason why the heirs are exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The duty to return רבית is not a normal theft obligation tied to the money. It is a personal command from the פסוק, 'so your brother may live with you.' That command falls on the lender alone, so his son is exempt, even though heirs in general are not like buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I can tell you (introduces holding on to one's position)
The Torah (the Merciful One) warns him

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the duty to return רבית is personal to the lender. It is not the same as the duty to return a stolen object.

phrases.english: Rava said: Actually, I will say to you

phrases.aramaic: רְשׁוּת יוֹרֵשׁ לָאו כִּרְשׁוּת לוֹקֵחַ דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: the domain of an heir is not like the domain of a buyer,
and here it is different, because the verse says:
"Take no interest or increase from him" –

phrases.aramaic: אַהְדַּר לֵיהּ, כִּי הֵיכִי דְּנֵחֵי בַּהֲדָךְ;
phrases.english: return it to him, so that he can live with you;
phrases.notes: This is read from the end of that same פסוק: 'so that your brother may live with you.'

phrases.english: the Merciful One warns him himself,
his son the Merciful One does not warn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference רמי בר חמא drew in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא. The ruling that heirs keep the רבית money still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The exemption comes from a special rule about רבית (the command is only on the lender), not from heirs being like buyers.

steps.title: How the two versions relate to each other
steps.stepSummary: If רמי בר חמא's rule was taught on the ברייתא, it applies all the more to the משנה. If it was taught on the משנה, then for the ברייתא רמי בר חמא would agree with רבא's explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who teaches it on the ברייתא would surely teach it on the משנה too. The one who teaches it on the משנה holds that, for the ברייתא, רמי בר חמא explains it the way רבא does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up how the two versions of רמי בר חמא's statement fit together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא can be explained without the heir-buyer rule, as רבא showed. The משנה has no such other explanation. So whoever learns the rule from the ברייתא would certainly learn it from the משנה. But whoever places it only on the משנה can say that רמי בר חמא accepts רבא's reason for the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who teaches it (on a certain source)

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree that רמי בר חמא holds an heir is like a buyer. They differ only on which source he learned it from. For the רבית ברייתא, רבא's reason works: only the lender himself is commanded to return the money.

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on the baraita –
all the more so on the mishna.
The one who teaches it on the mishna –
but on the baraita,

phrases.aramaic: רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא כְּרָבָא מַתְנֵי לַהּ.
phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama teaches it like Rava.
phrases.notes: He means that רמי בר חמא would also say the רבית case is special because of the פסוק, just as רבא said.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ אַבָּרַיְיתָא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַמַּתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up the two versions after רבא's rejection.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If the rule was taught on the ברייתא, it applies all the more to the משנה. If it was taught on the משנה, then רמי בר חמא explains the ברייתא with רבא's reason.

steps.title: A teaching about a thief whose children eat or inherit stolen food
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules on children of a thief. If he fed them stolen food, they are exempt. If he left it to them, גדולים must pay and קטנים are exempt. If the adults say they don't know their father's accounts with the owner, they are exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone steals and feeds the food to his children, the children do not have to pay. If he left it in front of them as an inheritance, adults must pay and minors do not. And if the adults say, 'We don't know what accounts our father settled with you,' they are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about what a thief's children owe for stolen food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three rulings. Children who were fed by their father owe nothing. Heirs who received the stolen food are split: גדולים pay and קטנים don't. The last ruling, that adults are exempt just by saying 'we don't know,' is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: He left it before them, as an inheritance
Accounts or calculations between two people

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who robs and feeds it to his children –
they are exempt from paying.
If he left it before them –
phrases.notes: He died and the stolen food passed to them as an inheritance.

phrases.english: adults are obligated to pay;
minors are exempt from paying.
And if the adults said:
We do not know the accounts
that our father settled with you – they are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַגּוֹזֵל וּמַאֲכִיל אֶת בָּנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא on the related theme of heirs and stolen property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Children fed stolen food are exempt. Heirs of stolen food: גדולים pay, קטנים are exempt. Adults who say 'we don't know our father's accounts' are exempt.

steps.title: How can 'we don't know' be enough to exempt them?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised. Heirs who received stolen goods cannot escape paying just by saying they don't know whether their father settled up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just because they say 'we don't know,' they are exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last ruling of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is clear the goods were stolen. A vague 'maybe our father paid, we don't know' seems far too weak to cancel a clear debt. So the ruling as written seems hard to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not know (an uncertain claim)

phrases.english: Because they say:
'We do not know' – they are exempt?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמְרִי: אֵין אָנוּ יוֹדְעִין פְּטוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the final ruling of the ברייתא in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that adult heirs are exempt when they say 'we don't know our father's accounts.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An uncertain claim should not cancel a clear obligation to pay for stolen goods.

steps.title: רבא: the heirs are sure their father paid
steps.stepSummary: רבא rereads the ברייתא. The heirs are exempt because they claim with certainty that they know their father's accounts and that nothing is still owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This is what the ברייתא means. Adults who said, 'We know the accounts our father settled with you, and nothing of yours was left with him at all,' are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by explaining the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of an uncertain 'we don't know,' the heirs make a certain claim: 'we know, and he paid you in full.' A confident claim like that is strong enough to exempt them, so the question goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means (rereading a source)

phrases.english: Rava said: This is what it is saying:
Adults who said:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹדְעִים אָנוּ חֶשְׁבּוֹנוֹת שֶׁחִשֵּׁב אָבִינוּ עִמָּךְ,
phrases.english: We know the accounts that our father settled with you,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא פָּשׁ לָךְ גַּבֵּיהּ וְלָא מִידֵּי – פְּטוּרִין.
phrases.english: and nothing of yours remained with him at all – they are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by rereading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The heirs were exempt just by saying 'we don't know.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The heirs are exempt only because they confidently claim the father paid everything.

steps.title: A second teaching: even minors must pay
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא agrees that children fed stolen food are exempt. But if he left it to them and they ate it, both גדולים and קטנים must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: If someone steals and feeds it to his children, they do not have to pay. If he left it before them and they ate it, both adults and minors must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא on the same case, which seems to make even minors liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא seems to disagree with the first one, which exempted קטנים. Here both adults and minors who ate inherited stolen food are obligated. This sets up the next question.

phrases.english: It is taught in another [ברייתא]:
One who robs and feeds his children – they are exempt from paying.
If he left it before them and they ate it –
whether adults or minors, they are obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ברייתא that seems to differ from step 5 about minors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Children fed stolen food are exempt. Heirs who ate inherited stolen food, whether adults or minors, must pay.

steps.title: How can minors be liable?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how קטנים can be obligated. Eating the food is at most like causing damage, and a minor is not liable for damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are minors obligated?! At worst, it should be no more than a case of causing damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second ברייתא's ruling that minors must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the minors ate the stolen food, they destroyed someone else's property. That is just damaging, and a קטן is not liable for damages he causes. So why would the ברייתא make them pay?

keyTerms.meaning: Let it be no more than

phrases.english: Are minors obligated?!
Let it be no more than a case where he caused damage!
phrases.notes: A minor who damages is exempt, so eating the food should not make him liable either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling in step 8 that minors must pay.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that minors who ate inherited stolen food are obligated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eating the food is only damaging, and minors are exempt from paying for damage.

steps.title: רב פפא: the food has not been eaten yet
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rereads the second ברייתא. It is talking about a case where the stolen food is still there, so both adults and minors must return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is what it means. If he left it before them and they have not yet eaten it, both adults and minors are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by changing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the food was eaten, a minor would be exempt, because eating is only damaging. But when the stolen item still exists, it is not theirs, so even a minor must give it back. 'Obligated' here means obligated to return it.

keyTerms.meaning: And they have not yet eaten them

steps.confusionAlert: Minors are not being made to pay for damages here. They only have to hand back a stolen item that still exists.
steps.whatToRemember: A קטן is exempt for food he already ate (that is only damage), but he must return stolen property that is still around.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: This is what it is saying:
If he left it before them and they have not yet eaten it –
whether adults or minors, they are obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9 by rereading the ברייתא of step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא made minors pay for food they already ate.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about food not yet eaten, which even minors must return.

steps.title: רבא's rules about a borrowed cow left to heirs
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules about a father who left his children a borrowed cow. They may use it for the rest of the loan period. If it dies by אונס, they are not liable. If they slaughtered and ate it thinking it was their father's, they pay the value of meat at a cheap price. If the father left land, they must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If their father left them a borrowed cow, they may use it for the whole loan period. If it died, they are not liable for an accident. If they thought it was their father's and slaughtered and ate it, they pay the value of meat at a cheap price. If their father left them land, they must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a set of rules about heirs who end up holding a cow their father borrowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heirs may keep using the cow as their father could, until the loan ends. A שואל is normally liable even for אונס, but that liability was their father's own, so the heirs don't pay for it. If they ate it by mistake, they pay only cheap meat value, since they acted innocently. If the father left land, the heirs must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Its accidents, damage no one could prevent

steps.whatToRemember: Heirs can use a borrowed item for the loan period, but they are not liable for אונס. If they ate it by mistake, they pay cheap meat value. If the father left land, they must pay.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: הִנִּיחַ לָהֶם אֲבִיהֶם פָּרָה שְׁאוּלָה –
phrases.english: Rava said: If their father left them a borrowed cow –
they may use it for the whole period of its loan.
If it died – they are not liable for its accidents.
If they thought it was their father's,
and they slaughtered it and ate it –
they pay the value of meat at a cheap price.
If their father left them guaranteed property –
phrases.notes: This means land, which a debt can be collected from.

phrases.english: they are obligated to pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הִנִּיחַ לָהֶם אֲבִיהֶם פָּרָה שְׁאוּלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from stolen items left to heirs to a borrowed item left to heirs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Heirs may use a borrowed cow for the loan period. They are not liable for its אונס. If they ate it by mistake, they pay cheap meat value. If the father left land, they must pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a borrower's special liability for accidents is personal and does not pass to his heirs, unless the father left land.

steps.title: Two versions of where the land rule belongs
steps.stepSummary: Some attach רבא's land rule to the first case (death by אונס), and others attach it to the last case (heirs ate the cow).
steps.simpleTranslation: Some teach this line on the first part, and some teach it on the last part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says there are two versions of where רבא's final line about land belongs. This sets up the next step, which explains what each version means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's ruling had two parts. The cow dying by אונס means the heirs are exempt, and the heirs eating it means they pay a cheap meat price. The line "if the father left land, they must pay" could go on the first part, so they pay even for אונס, or only on the last part, so they pay the full value of what they ate.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who teach it (another version of the teaching)
The first clause of a teaching
The last clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: The two versions are not arguing about what רבא said. They are arguing about which of his cases the land line is attached to.

phrases.english: Some teach it on the first clause,
phrases.notes: "It" is רבא's last line: if the father left land, the heirs must pay. The first clause is the cow dying by אונס.

phrases.english: and some teach it on the last clause.
phrases.notes: The last clause is where the heirs slaughtered the cow and ate it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the scope of רבא's final clause from step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are two traditions about which case of רבא the land rule applies to.

steps.title: What each version means and how it relates to רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: Putting the land rule on the first case means it surely applies to the last case too, and that version argues with רב פפא. Putting it only on the last case fits רב פפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever teaches it on the first part would surely say it about the last part too, and this argues with רב פפא. Whoever teaches it on the last part does not say it about the first part, and this fits רב פפא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how far each version reaches and points out that one version disagrees with רב פפא while the other agrees with him. This sets up the quote from רב פפא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the heirs must pay from the land even when the cow died by אונס, then surely they pay when they ate it themselves. That is a כל שכן. The first version holds that a borrower's duty to pay for אונס starts from the moment of borrowing, so the father's land was already tied to the debt. רב פפא holds that the duty only starts when the damage happens, so the father was never obligated and the heirs owe nothing for אונס.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is the same as (it fits)

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on the first clause —
all the more so on the last clause,
and this argues with Rav Pappa.
The one who teaches it on the last clause —
but on the first clause, not,
and this fits Rav Pappa.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ אַרֵישָׁא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the consequences of the two versions given in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The version on the first clause covers both cases and argues with רב פפא. The version on the last clause covers only that case and fits רב פפא.

steps.title: רב פפא on a stolen cow versus a borrowed cow slaughtered on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A thief who slaughters a stolen cow on שבת must pay, because his theft came first. A borrower who slaughters a borrowed cow on שבת is exempt, because the theft and the שבת sin happen at the same moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: If he had a stolen cow and slaughtered it on שבת, he must pay, because he was already responsible for the theft before he broke שבת. If he had a borrowed cow and slaughtered it on שבת, he is exempt, because breaking שבת and stealing come together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רב פפא's rule to show why the second version fits him. A borrower only becomes responsible at the moment he does something wrong with the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who does a sin punishable by death, like slaughtering on שבת, is not also made to pay money for that same act. A thief was already liable from the moment he stole, before שבת came into the picture, so he pays. A borrower only becomes a thief when he slaughters the cow, which is the same moment as the שבת sin, so he is exempt. This shows that for רב פפא, the borrower's liability is not "locked in" from the time of borrowing.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that, according to רב פפא, a borrower's responsibility starts only when the damage happens. That is why heirs are not liable for a cow that died by אונס after their father died.
steps.whatToRemember: The question of when liability starts decides everything. A thief is liable from the moment he steals, but a borrower is liable only when the damage happens.

phrases.english: As Rav Pappa said:
If he had a stolen cow,
and he slaughtered it on Shabbat — he is liable;
because he was already liable for the theft,
before he came to the Shabbat prohibition.
If he had a borrowed cow,
and he slaughtered it on Shabbat — he is exempt;
because the Shabbat prohibition and the theft prohibition
come as one.
phrases.notes: Slaughtering the borrowed cow is the very act that makes him a thief, so both sins happen at the same moment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source of רב פפא's view mentioned in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stolen cow slaughtered on שבת must be paid for, but a borrowed cow slaughtered on שבת is exempt, because the borrower's theft starts only with the slaughter.

steps.title: A new ברייתא: return the very item that was robbed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the words "אשר גזל" that the robber must return the same item he stole.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: "He shall return the stolen item that he robbed." Why does the פסוק add "that he robbed"? To teach that he must return it just as he stole it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new ברייתא that learns a rule from the extra words of a פסוק. This opens a new discussion, so the learner should expect it to continue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have just said "return the stolen item," so the extra words "אשר גזל" must teach something. The ברייתא learns that the robber should return the actual item, in the same form he took it, when it is still there. The ruling for heirs will grow out of this ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the פסוק come to teach?
Like what he robbed (the same item)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And he shall return the stolen item that he robbed";
Why does the verse say "that he robbed"?
He should return it like what he robbed.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת הַגְּזֵילָה אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the borrowed-cow discussion and opens a new ברייתא about returning stolen property, which ties back to the earlier ברייתות about heirs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From "אשר גזל" we learn that the robber must return the same item he robbed.

steps.title: Robber's children who ate the stolen food versus children who inherited it
steps.stepSummary: From 'אשר גזל' the חכמים learn that a robber's children who ate the stolen food are exempt. If the item was left to them, they must return it. סומכוס says only adults must return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here they said: if someone robs and feeds the food to his children, the children do not have to pay. If he left the stolen item to them, they must return it, whether they are adults or minors. In the name of סומכוס they said: adults must return it, minors do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its teaching from step 15 and applies the rule 'return the same item' to the robber's children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The obligation is to return the actual stolen item. If the children ate it, it is gone, so they have nothing to return and are exempt. If the item still exists in the inheritance, they hold the stolen thing itself and must give it back. סומכוס adds an exception for minors.

keyTerms.meaning: From here they said (a rule learned from the פסוק just quoted)
He left it to them (as an inheritance)

steps.confusionAlert: Eating the food does not make the children exempt as a favor to them. They are exempt because the stolen item no longer exists for them to return.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule for heirs of a robber that the coming sugya keeps using.

phrases.english: From here they said:
phrases.notes: 'From here' means from 'אשר גזל' in step 15: what must be returned is the very thing that was stolen.

phrases.english: One who robs and feeds it to his children —
they are exempt from paying.
If he left it before them —
phrases.notes: He means the stolen item is still there when the children inherit it.

phrases.english: whether adults or minors, they are obligated.
In the name of Sumakhos they said:
Adults are obligated; minors are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws practical rules for heirs from the derivation of 'אשר גזל' in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Children who ate stolen food are exempt. Children who inherited the existing stolen item must return it. סומכוס exempts minors.

steps.title: Story: רבי ירמיה is shut out by his brother-in-law
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה's brother-in-law shut the door on him, and רבי ירמיה took the case to רבי אבין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The son of רבי ירמיה's father-in-law slammed the door in רבי ירמיה's face. רבי ירמיה came before רבי אבין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about a dispute over property in the family. This line sets up the case for the court discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The brother-in-law blocked רבי ירמיה from property that had belonged to the brother-in-law's father. רבי ירמיה claims a right to it, so he goes to court.

keyTerms.meaning: Son of his father-in-law, meaning his brother-in-law

phrases.english: The son of Rabbi Yirmeya's father-in-law
slammed the door in Rabbi Yirmeya's face.
He came before Rabbi Avin.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּר חֲמוּהּ דְּרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה טְרַק גַּלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related story about heirs and property after the rules about a robber's heirs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the brother-in-law blocks רבי ירמיה, and רבי ירמיה brings the case to רבי אבין.

steps.title: רבי אבין: the brother-in-law is claiming his own property
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין rules that the brother-in-law is claiming what belongs to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין said: he is claiming what is his.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבין gives his first ruling: the brother-in-law has the stronger position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The property was the brother-in-law's father's, so the son is treated as its owner by inheritance. רבי ירמיה would need to prove otherwise.

keyTerms.meaning: He is claiming what is his own

phrases.english: He said: He is claiming what is his.
phrases.notes: רבי אבין is speaking. He means the son holds his father's property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the judge's response to the case brought in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The heir is presumed to own his father's property.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה offers witnesses that he took possession earlier
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה objects that he can bring witnesses showing he took possession while the father was alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said to him: But I can bring witnesses that I took possession of it during his father's lifetime!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה pushes back against רבי אבין's ruling by offering proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he took possession while the father was still alive, the property never passed to the son by inheritance. That would cancel the son's claim of ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: I took possession of it (made a legal acquisition)

phrases.english: He said to him:
But I can bring witnesses
that I took possession of it in his father's lifetime!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אבין's ruling from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבין's ruling that the brother-in-law owns the property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnesses could show that רבי ירמיה acquired the property before the father died, so the son never inherited it.

steps.title: רבי אבין questions whether the witnesses can be accepted
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין starts to answer by asking whether the court may accept such witnesses at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין said to him: But does the court accept witnesses...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבין begins to push back on רבי ירמיה's offer of witnesses. His question continues in the next lines of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבין does not argue with the facts the witnesses would report. He questions whether the court is allowed to hear these witnesses in this situation. The condition he means is spelled out as the sentence continues.

keyTerms.meaning: But does the court accept witnesses?

phrases.english: He said to him:
But do we accept witnesses

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof רבי ירמיה offered in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The witnesses רבי ירמיה wants to bring
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Questions whether the court may accept these witnesses at all. The full reason continues in the next lines.
